reviewer: Independent reviewer (Claude Opus 5 CLI documentation review seat)

fixture.providerMode: dedicated local OpenID Connect fixture; full browser authorization and callback; no external identity-provider account

steps.action: An unreachable issuer fails discovery and registers no provider
steps.actual: Registering an issuer on a port with no OpenID configuration was refused. The pane reported "The change could not be saved. Try again." beside the control, no provider was recorded, and the mode stayed built_in. The guide instruction to correct the issuer URL or its reachability and retry matches what the pane does, though the message itself does not name discovery as the cause.

steps.action: Registration completed the switch and fixed the Provider ID
steps.actual: Successful registration completed the pending switch: the mode is oidc with provider helix-idp. The pane now offers Save provider instead of Register provider and no longer exposes a Provider ID field, so the guide statement that the Provider ID is fixed after registration holds. The client secret hint reads "Leave blank to keep the current secret."

steps.action: An invited colleague signs in through the identity provider and keeps the invited role
steps.actual: Tomas Novak, invited as Contributor and never activated by password, pressed Continue with single sign-on, completed the identity provider authorization and returned through the OpenLaw callback, landing at http://127.0.0.1:43328/. His account kept role contributor and became Active. The identity provider established identity while OpenLaw kept the role it already held, which is what the guide claims.

steps.action: An Administrator keeps password sign-in while OIDC is selected
steps.actual: With the mode set to OIDC, Administrator sign-in on the sign-in page opened the password form and the first-run password worked. This is the break-glass route the guide tells an Administrator to keep available while testing single sign-on, and the recovery path back to Built-in.

steps.action: A non-Administrator cannot use password sign-in while single sign-on is required
steps.actual: A Contributor using the same Administrator password form while single sign-on is required was refused with "Password sign-in is disabled while single sign-on is required." and stayed on the auth pages. Only the Administrator keeps password sign-in in OIDC mode.

steps.action: Saving a changed field with a blank client secret keeps the stored secret
steps.actual: Changing Client ID while leaving Client secret blank saved successfully, and the pane displayed the callback URL http://127.0.0.1:43328/api/auth/sso/callback again, ending in /api/auth/sso/callback on the instance address. A complete single sign-on round trip still reached http://127.0.0.1:43328/ afterwards, so the blank field kept the stored secret rather than clearing it, exactly as the guide says. Note that Save provider with nothing changed is a silent no-op that sends no request.

steps.action: Supplying a replacement secret rotates it and sign-in still completes
steps.actual: Pasting a replacement Client secret and saving succeeded, the field cleared itself again afterwards so the secret is never shown back, and a further complete single sign-on round trip reached http://127.0.0.1:43328/. This is the rotation the guide describes. The local fixture accepts the client secret without enforcing a real provider policy, so this verifies OpenLaw's own handling only.

steps.action: A failed issuer update leaves the previous provider configuration usable
steps.actual: Saving an unreachable issuer was refused with the field error, the stored provider still carried the working issuer http://docs-idp:43329, and a complete single sign-on round trip still reached http://127.0.0.1:43328/. The guide hedge that a failed update should leave the previous provider configuration available is what actually happened.

steps.action: Restore the working client identifier for the remaining checks
In OIDC mode the magic-link switch is editable and can be turned off
steps.actual: Unlike built-in mode the switch was enabled in OIDC mode, with the hint "Turn off to require SSO for everyone." Turning it off saved: the resolved magicLinkEnabled became false. The corrected guide describes exactly this contrast between the two modes.

steps.action: With magic links off the Portal offers single sign-on instead of an emailed link
steps.actual: With magic links off the Portal entry page no longer offered Send link. It read: "OpenLaw Legal request portal Sign-in links are switched off. Use your organization's sign-in to reach the portal. Sign in Help with this page". Requesters must use the organisation identity provider, which is why the guide warns they then need suitable identity-provider accounts.

steps.action: An existing Business User still enters the Portal through single sign-on
steps.actual: With magic links off, the Portal entry page read "Sign-in links are switched off" and offered Sign in, which led to Continue with single sign-on. An existing Business User completed the identity provider round trip and reached http://127.0.0.1:43328/portal. Turning magic links off does not disable OIDC Portal entry, which is what the guide states.

steps.action: Recovery: an Administrator returns the instance to built-in sign-in
steps.actual: Selecting Built-in returned the mode immediately. Magic links were switched back on and the switch became disabled again, so the built-in floor reasserts itself rather than leaving the previous OIDC choice in place. The Portal entry page offered Send link once more and a real sign-in link was delivered. This is the recovery route the guide gives an Administrator who needs to undo a single sign-on change.
